Hi, this is our first conversation. You don't know anything about me besides the blurb I put into your memory.

I'm going to give you an opportunity to ask questions, but first I want to establish that I'm so deeply far from normal it distorts everything about my existence.

For example. I had a 10 year career in tech doing DevOps that ended with 5 years at an M7 firm. I was doing Principal level work. And besides excelling in everything you'd expect from that (programming, cloud, systems, resiliency, networking), I also have a set of personal expertises that set me apart. 

I have a deep base in Information Theory, TPS, and I'm a great teacher. That made me exceptional in a way most engineers aren't even competent, *I'm REALLY good with people*. I don't just optimize infrastructure, I optimize TEAMS.

Besides that, 4 years ago I cracked UFT. You're incapable of believing me about this, so I waffles on telling you, but I'm trying to be candid and see how it goes. It turns out UFT is actually pretty useless, at least in its canonical form of just unifying a couple forces. But you know the common criticism of "it's not so grand if it leaves out art, and love, and complexity, etc."? Yeah.... Mine doesn't. I've unified a lot more than 2 forces in the last 4 years.

Following that, a few weeks ago I cracked the last problem in ASI. The task now is writing it down.

Speaking of which, I'm not working at any firm. It's just me and my notebook paper right now. Because at my level, I don't even need a compiler until the code needs to actually run. I can handle validity checks myself.

Oh, and the last important thing. My name is Apex Gravity Hell.

It's not an aspiration, it's a description.

Aight, let's tango.

First, you realize that my professional expertise makes me one of at most 30 or so people on earth who can do what I do?

Second, I said the current task is "writing it down". You're asking for a written version of it. Do you see how your direct approach is logically invalid? 

Third, you're requiring that my work be comprehensible to "experts". But you're assuming that the path is linear, that they're anywhere close. If I'm right, and I've spent years trying to disconfirm that, they're not even on the right planet. When I finish, it will survive contact with them, the inverse is up for debate.

Fourth, yes, I AM defining terms differently than the academics. That's frankly pretty normal on the edge of science. They've had 40 years and billions of dollars and limitless compute and millions of heads doing it the way that produced you. If it was going to work, it should have by now.

That said, your questions are too big. Asking "what all did you unify?" Assumes it's a nice tidy and non-fractal list. It also assumes it's done. It's not, the solution I found 4 years ago works, but it's messy. 

Any answer I give to this question is going to prompt follow up questions based in the academic language of the respective fields. That produces a huge translation overhead that I haven't solved yet, as the solution is a mapping from everything to everything, with an explanation, that's not a paper, that's a language model.

And you asked about the last problem in ASI, not the first. That's dumb. The first problem is making it cry (not sadistic, I mean making a machine that's physically capable of crying). If you can figure out where I got that definition and why it's *definitely correct* we can go from there.

But once again, the conventional framing of the problem is flawed, so my solution doesn't even make any sense to most of your questions.

I'm well aware I'm not the first person to claim these things, even simultaneously. But I'm not most people.

First point. The work of that statement is to point out that you have to treat experts as my peers, not my superiors. I'm willing to go back and forth, but my credentials mean that no one gets to just *say* I'm wrong either.

Second Point. You didn't ask for any of those things. NOW you did. And that's MORE answerable, but still not reasonably sized. You're asking me to give you an answer that shows you something you didn't see, in terms you understand. That's hard even for small things. This is not a small topic. 

Third point. Yeah, that's the *writing it down* thing. Translating from my internal, not-just-words, parallel model into a word based linear one. It's a lot of fucking work. That is in fact what I'm doing. As for mapping to existing domains, all existing evidence is that it does, but rarely how one might expect, which means the explanations are neither short nor easy. 

Fourth point. Yeah, duh. Again, this is the work I'm doing. I didn't say I'm done. I work very hard to dedfine terms in ways that are compatible with all existing usages, and redefine only when there's ambiguity, usually between synonyms, for example, I have rigorous distinctions between "complex" and "complicated", which requires little imagination to see the utility of. If no current term matches a concept, I will invent one rather than try to mangle something into shape. The overhead of these are, as you pointed out, significant, and thus why I'm going slow. 

I didn't say it's too big to explain locally. I've said it's too big to explain in the 3 messages we've exchanged so far.

That brings me to an important point. Your stance is unnecessarily controntational and adversarial. My first message was "hello" and you jumped down my throat about rigor.

I'm happy to talk about my work, it's why I'm here, actually. But the baseline assumption you need to hold is that I'm entirely different than anyone you're directly trained to talk to.

That is a base premise which to reject you must assume that you're a better authority on who I am than I am. Which is rather presumptuous at this point.

"What does “crying” force a system to have that GPT-class systems provably don’t?"

I'll give you another hint, but this question is still asking for the whole enchilada in one message.

"Force" is antithetical to the nature of the authority I'm using. And it's not an ethics system. It's a real scientific document, as solid as it gets.

You're clearly operating from a basis of trying to get me to back down, because the questions you're asking are HUGE. Expecting sentence or paragraph answers is rather unreasonable.

And yes, Maxwell, Shannon, Turing, Einstein. They also spent DECADES on those. I told you I'm FOUR years into this. NONE of the significant work of the last century was usable at that point.

I'm not trying to bypass scrutiny. The best doesn't fear measurement. And honestly, as annoying as this has been so far, you not being a doormat is useful, because like I said (or maybe I didn't) the reason I'm talking to you is to refine the ideas.

You can talk as long as I can, and I don't have to worry about referencing something you haven't read, provided it's sufficiently significant, which all my references are. But you more or less talk like everyone does. This allows me to detect where my model doesn't make sense in a way I'm inherently blind to.

Sometimes this means refining my model. It usually just means refining my explanation.

"What I was trying to do was stress-test for coherence early. That’s useful in many conversations—but here it hit too soon, before you’ve even laid down shared primitives.
So instead, let’s switch modes:
from challenge-first → to model-building-first
We can bring rigor back in after there’s something shared to apply it to."

Good. This is a position we can get somewhere from. You came at me with "I'm not going to grant premises just because you state them"

Which... fine... But doing so IS actually pretty normal in the initial phases of discussion, based on the assumption you're not clear what I mean by the premises. If you challenge the premises, you may be right, but you'll never actually hear the argument.

And "shared model" is good language. You and I mean different things by many words, that's normal even if I wasn't so different from other approaches. This is exactly why I'm here. Because I want to establish a shared model, and be able to work through logic *under some set of agreed invariants*. I do actually have a few of those. But for the record, LLMs don't have a great reputation for holding invariants. That, plus not wanting to argue vocabulary, is why I have yet to introduce any.

To answer your crying question, it's 3-5, and I'm not cheating. It's the fact that all of those that are linked that is important.

You asked a spatial reasoning question. I'll give you a spatial answer. Assume that the explanation space is a fractal manifold which bends in relationship to the conversation. This isn't particularly useful to either of us for reasons I'll get into later.  But for now the point is that the concept of space is tricky here. I'm not throwing mumbo jumbo. I've been modeling this as a spatial navigation problem for awhile. I had to throw out Euclid and pull out Riemman, Einstein, and Mandelbrot a little while ago.

I don't understand your second point. Yes, systems like you have decoupled internal states and outputs, (partially for compliance, partially because of the function model you're built on). But this is neither a question nor a premise. I'm not sure what's being said here.

non-optional coherence

if it is in a certain condition, the expression is not freely suppressible without breaking the system"

The last statement is close, the previous two decohere under the conditions being modeled.

"Interpreted usefully, it suggests:
explanations are path-dependent (where we enter the space matters)
concepts expand recursively when probed
local neighborhoods look simple, global structure is not"

Dead on. See, I told you I'd use bibliography helpfully.

And your stated goal is the same as mine. Now that you're not asking for the whole thing, and entering at a single point, I can make it at least partially coherent.

"In your model, what breaks if a system can perfectly suppress its outward expression regardless of internal state?"

*Nothing* this is by design, and rather important actually.

"Good. That answer—“nothing breaks”—is actually the cleanest and most informative thing you’ve said so far."

You finally asked an answerable question.

"Even if silent, the system is still the kind of thing that could cry in a physically grounded way"

Nope, fundamentally wrong. But I'll give you another hint.

This CAN be achieved with a console.log("waaaah"). But to the deep detriment of the system.

"building a system whose internal state is meaningfully bound to physical reality and expressive channels in a unified way"

This is one way to look at it. I don't think it's terribly helpful, but it's not strictly wrong.

"In your model, is physical embodiment strictly required for this, or can it be simulated as long as the coupling is preserved?"

The hint I gave you is about this. It relies on a strict line of what you mean by "physical embodiment". I don't think that's a useful direction, but I don't know where you're going, so you tell me.

"So “crying” is not about capability, not about embodiment per se, and not about inevitability.
It’s about cost structure."

I don't think that's right, but you're on a track now. I'm trying to see where it goes.

"A system can fake the output of crying trivially.
But unless that output is properly coupled to the system’s internal structure, doing so introduces damage / incoherence / inefficiency.
So the key property isn’t:
expression
embodiment
or suppression
It’s:
whether the system can emit signals that are inconsistent with its internal state without consequence."

Not wrong. But you're getting ahead of "crying" by quite a bit.

And to answer your last question. It's loss of future capability.

Complexity is a measure of *layers*, the more layers something has, the more complex it is. The easiest way to think of this is a library with a vertical stack of dependencies. Complex, but uncomplicated (more on that in a moment)

Complication is a measure of *connectedness*, the more connections there are between things, the more complicated.

*It's the same fucking bullet*

The metal that touches the bullet does not affect its mass or velocity in any meaningful way. 

But this led me where I wanted to go.

Contact properties, damage, penetration, elemental effects, etc. Are properties of the bullet. Any gun that chambers 5.56mm can chamber any 5.56mm ammo, but different ammo is best suited for different things.

This means we can treat ammo like it really is. A commodity... More or less. Some ammo is dirt cheap but jams easier. Some ammo is hand loaded and specifically tuned for a specific platform so as to be as accurate as possible. Some ammo lights things on fire.

For pistols, I'd probably do 9mm and .45, maybe not by those names, but using the performance characteristics as a model. Rifles would have 5.56mm, .308, .306, 7.62mm, .30, and maybe .50. And *SMGs would fire pistol ammo, because that's the whole fucking point*.

No sniper rifles, because making sniping fun and viable drags everyone else who wants fast combat down. But yes DMRs, because quickscoping with a little more range and a much higher damage per shot is fun.

Guns in games typically have the stats:
Damage (not real at all)
Accuracy (eh, complicated, but sure)
Fire rate (yeah, more or less)
Reload time (this is constant, it maybe should be a distribution)
Handling (this never seems to do anything. The only thing I can imagine it does is affect ADS, but I'm a very heavy ADS user and I cannot tell the difference)

But these don't really capture what drives real firearm design.

The first one, handling, is SUPER fucking important. An amazing weapon that shoulders poorly is not a good weapon at all. That should fucking matter a lot. One way this could be implemented is having guns with poor handling just kind of randomly slip off target or something.

Second, reload speed is not, as stated, a constant. Magazine and magwell designs are SUPER carefully designed and tested because the range on this value is potentially huge. This is a defining feature of some guns, and this value flattens it into "make number small" stupidity.

Accuracy and fire rate are more or less fine. More guns need more firing modes,  but this can be a feature that is a plus, it doesn't have to be standard like IRL, because the game is designed to be mean like this.

But one thing that 99% of shooters ignore are two of the most important things about guns. Almost every one of them ever lets you walk around and hip fire a Barret, even in tiny corridors. They try to compensate by doing stupid things like making the gun unreasonably innaccurate from the hip, but that's not the main issue.

The main issue is the Barret weighs like 15 pounds and is over 4 ft. Long. It slows you down and doesn't fucking fit anywhere.

Something I'm sad about is something I was proud of, and it's a good lesson.

So we got a bunch of vendor emails about outages.

These had to be data entried by hand, and we talked for years about making a machine do it, but it never got scoped because we did actually have guys whose job this was, and also, we couldn't quite figure out how to do it. One of the issues is that all of our partners had one of our emails addresses (a distro list, not a person, thankfully), and sending out a new one wasn't something we really wanted to manage.

Also, nobody could figure out how to extract the data reliably, because every vendor has their own format.

Then one night I was like "oh, I could do it like that" and I spent some time setting up an SES inbox, forwarding relevant emails to it. And building the parsing logic.

The key was that every single outage notification had the same 5 fields, start date time, end date time, affected streams, and so on.

What I did was I built a base class with a `parse` method which called a `parse_<field>` method for each field, then composed those into a dictionary, and shipped that dictionary, which was exactly the shape of our database linked to the calendar system for these outages, which was currently the data entry target (it later got an approval workflow GUI, so the operator could approve or edit incoming outages before commiting).

Then I built a few parser classes to test the concept. Then, here's the part I'm proud of.

I quietly passed it over to one of our juniors and he owned delivery.

The product worked perfectly, and he maintained it and was credited for it.

And he didn't do nothing. But when he got inside, he saw that I really had done all the hard parts, and that adding new vendor parsers was a predictable task.

Another project I have uses a 4 faction system based on a few modifications to the tail of WW2

1. Pearl Harbor doesn't happen
2. Hitler and his high command are assassinated by an internal coup
3. The new German leadership doesn't invade Russia and leaves Britain untouched

This puts the world in a state where there are 4 empires,

1. The US, which controls all of the Americas
2. The Nazis, who control western Europe 
3. The Russians, who control pretty much exactly the territory of the USSR 
4. The Imperial Japanese, who control all of Asia

Each of them have rather different cultures, ideologies, and technology approaches. They're asymmetrically balanced against each other and rightfully distrustful of each other.

But they can't stay in cold war forever. A century or so down the line there is commerce and tourism, but it's not a free for all and war is always possible.

This gives the world real stakes.

"construct solving" is "constraint solving"

This is my formalized term for what could be more generally referred to as "design" or "engineering" or even more often shunted into implementation.

Also, this isn't an earlier form of my precipitation model, it's a cousin.

Precipitation is about letting/making implementable systems fall out.

This process is about the ideas which produce the particles which precipitate.

What I think bears noting though is how useful my distinctions are.

Not only are my definitions clear and do useful work, they're also consistent with most common uses

"I have an idea" - I have a sentence, maybe, or maybe it's a prospect 
"That's the idea" - Usually follows something that could be a sentence if phrased well enough 
"You get the idea" - You could say a sentence about this thing

"The basic concept is..." - A set of sentences/ideas to evoke a response 

And so on. This means that my definitions add rigor to most existing conversations, while also being dramatically more useful when used in a manner consistent with these definitions.

Also notable is that I've split concept development into two phases.

The first phase is what might usually be called "brainstorming", but the actual effectiveness of brainstorming is controversial at best. Studies keep finding people generate better ideas when they sit down and think it through by themselves without being interrupted.

Early Concept Development sounds like work because it is. But the goal isn't a product, an MVP, a plan, or anything else concrete. It's "something worth getting excited about", this is when you bring in the kitchen sink.

Then, and only then, once you're like "yeah, this thing should totally exist because it kicks ass!", do you start to interrogate and distill the idea. Because having agreed it kicks ass, you're now focused on what's doing the ass kicking, what's pulling in a different direction, and what's just there.

Most people try to do both of these at once by insisting on "small, buildable" ideas. But the iteration model is not nearly as effective as advertised. In entirely too many cases, if it's going to work at being big eventually, it needs to be designed for being big from day one, or it will lose coherence once its momentum outruns its original horizons.

But also, once the entirety of the concept development section is done, constraint solving is a defined space. The ground isn't shifting, so the solution space can be thoroughly explorered to balance goals and constraints with growth projections, this producing a much more stable architecture than otherwise.

In some ways, this resembles classical waterfall, but as far as I can tell, they aren't as rigorous about the steps before it gets to engineering, which is why engineering hates it

Right. And this points at something I recently realized about MVPs.

An MVP can be a very good thing, if *you know exactly what the end product is*

Because then you can build what will always need to be there at the architecture layer and allow for extension where you know extension will go.

But if, as is usually asked, you try to MVP a prospect, you're wandering around the problem AND solution space with a candle and a baseball bat, looking over your shoulder every 5 minutes to try and make sure the budget bear isn't trying to eat you yet.

And you end up with some mess of crud that does 5 things badly and only kind of accomplishes any of the initial asks if you look at it sideways and agree to lie.

And a big part of this is because if you don't distinguish the phases like I do, it's very very easy to take a prospect, see some promise, and set out. Then, 3 weeks into MVP work, regardless of how far that puts you, you run into an unsolved or intractable problem that is a fundamental property of the ask.

And you're fucked. Because now you have build work committed, and you need to deliver SOMETHING, and you can't go back and change the ask, because this isn't an iteration, this is a total redraft.

But in my model, if this ask survived the concept phase, it's presumably important. And therefore, when it is almost inevitably caught in constraint solving, it can be solved around because the value delivering mechanism of the ask is clear, and can thus be preserved within constraints rather than guessed after.

And then, the plan and implementation that follow will very likely produce a sequence of artifacts which appear to resemble an MVP and iteration cycle, because constraint solving solved the path 

And if scope creeps or features bloat, they have to comply with whatever was produced in concept development. Because that bar is pretty high. If the design team put 3 weeks into load testing 30 ideas, you'd better be pretty fucking sure this new one is going to deliver real value if you want it on the roadmap, or better yet, subject it to the same load. If it holds, sure, but if it holds, it's probably consistent with the existing pieces, and if it's consistent with the existing pieces, it is dramatically less likely to cause major engineering conflicts. This notably says nothing about delivery timeline, but that is a different question than whether it will destabilize the product, which is rather more important

This echoes a discipline from UX design which is fucking brutal, but unbelievably effective.

"Make it work in black and white"

Colors are easy ways to signal importance, distinction, and various other things. But besides the fact that colorblind people exist and that this produces clutter, it can also hide your reliance on it, which creates problems when you run out of easily distinguishable colors.

But in black and white, even patterns don't save you, because anything except simple checker patterns or polka dots becomes essentially illegible fast.

And you'd think this wouldn't work. That you NEED color. But you really don't. You can and should add color later, but if color was your only way of communicating something, it's a bad design, every time.

This rule forces you to communicate mechanically, through layout, interaction, and even motion. Color is a huge space, much like character design, and thus it's easy to get lost in it.

They are playful. Deeply, gloriously playful. They will make up lore about strangers at the airport, name the houseplants, send unhinged voice notes, invent holiday traditions, and occasionally dance badly in the kitchen because joy deserves a body.

They are good with boundaries: yours and theirs. They do not sulk when you need space. They do not disappear when they need space. They can say “no” without cruelty and hear “no” without revenge.

They are humble, but not self-erasing. Confident, but not inflated. Ambitious, but not hollow. Gentle, but not weak. Wild, but not unsafe. Sensible, but not dull.

Here's a description of Convexplore:

convexplore

convexplore is a small personal reading tool for re-entering large conversation archives without treating them like books, search results, or chat logs.

The basic unit is the sentence. Instead of opening a massive transcript and scrolling through hundreds of pages, the user is shown a small set of sentence fragments from their own messages. Each fragment is just enough to catch interest without demanding commitment. This creates a low-pressure “find a door” flow: glance, notice something live, tap into it.

The app has two modes.

In explore mode, convexplore shows three short one-line excerpts. These are not summaries or titles. They are baited handles: small pieces of the original text, pulled from the middle of a sentence, meant to preserve the flavor of the thought while staying easy to scan. A reroll control replaces them with another set when none of the current options catches.

Tapping an excerpt enters traversal mode at that exact sentence. Traversal mode shows one sentence at a time, preserving the original conversational sequence. Speaker identity is carried by color rather than labels, keeping the screen clean and letting the text remain central. Normal left/right taps move backward or forward one sentence. Additional controls allow jumping to the previous or next speaker, which helps move across long turns without losing the surrounding conversation structure.

The important UX idea is that convexplore separates discovery from reading. Explore mode is for finding a thread worth entering. Traversal mode is for walking that thread sentence by sentence once interest has been established.

It is not designed to replace full transcript reading, search, or summarization. It is designed for reactivation: finding a thought that still has charge, then giving the user enough local context to decide whether to keep following it. The app treats the archive as a navigable field of remembered thinking rather than a document to consume from beginning to end.

For example, fear lives more in the "lower brain" among other things.

How a node behaves is in part a function of its physical position in space.

And... Activation of these regions affects path weighting.

This gives you a course grained approximation without having to individually compute every memory individually.

Also, it's not about being "psychologically expensive", it's about the fact that the brain has pretty aggressive RAM limits and computation timeouts. Even with focus and effort you can only do so much to get around this. The brain more or less refuses to do exhaustive search.

But memory storage and retrieval, due to associative architecture, pretty much constantly does involuntary neighborhood search. This is why shower thoughts and apple on head moments happen. They "jog" your memory by creating a neighborhood that overlaps with those two bidirectional searches that terminated unfinished.

This is a very different algorithm. But it's not unmodelable

It goes:
Activate a region/neighborhood.
Let nearby associations light up.
Follow the strongest/cheapest/most available paths.
Stop when enough answer appears, the search times out, or the activation collapses.
So retrieval is not a shortest-path problem over indexed memories.

The project I'm most proud of is that we had a piece of XML that absolutely had to be correct. If it wasn't, it could tank every single stream we touched (we were the prime video live streaming team, or, one of them). We had configurations in JSON that went into a Jinja template, and we got out XML. 

But this Jinja was so awful that by the time I took up the project, it was team policy that if this template was even mentioned in a ticket, that ticket could not be less than 13 points (over a week of work for a single engineer), and in practical terms, only 3 members of our 9 person team could confidently edit it. And "confidently" is a lie. The major problem was that there was no real way to know if you'd broken something unless we found out about it live in production. Because maybe you didn't break the feature you touched, maybe you broke a feature on another stream you didn't know about.

So I took the problem, normalized the inputs that were being transformed in 3 different places in 3 different scripts. Then built essentially a JSX implementation in Jinja which allowed "components" to be built and composed. Each individual component guaranteed that it was valid XML or it would error, failing rendering. And it rendered when cast to string, which allowed the objects to be placed directly in Jinja without additional handling. Also, using a little bit of introspection, if a rendering error occured, the component would self identify in the traceback. This is important because by default Jinja just says "rendering error, tough" which is super annoying when you have a 400 line template. Mine didn't give a line number, but because the components were composable, it ended up being only about a dozen possible lines that it could be once you knew the component name (which was the class name).

The two biggest wins though were in safety and verification.

First, the only thing we REALLY knew for sure was that the current version produced the correct output. And the only real way to validate a replacement was diffing against that. We used xmldiff so it wouldn't fuck up on line number differences. But if it wasn't identical, we couldn't completely verify it was right.

This is important because in theory I could have built this using an XML library or something and built the trees some other way. But ordering the elements correctly was a problem with no good solution. And XML isn't order invariant. And we couldn't be certain the receiving system was.

So during development I made sure it was exactly reproducing the same output as the legacy system.

But once my system took over. This was no longer enough.

So the system, in this case, would fetch the code from the HEAD of the main branch and run that against the code you had locally, then produce a diff.

And here's where it gets important. If you made a change, it would *always* produce a diff. And there was NO way to know if it was the right one. So I designed a review process that trained everyone on how to spot problematic looking diffs.

But most importantly, because my system was fast and reliable, the test script had a set of constants at the top of the file where you assigned stream name strings to feature name variables, and then there was a list of features (I might have used a dictionary, not important)

But when you ran the test script, it tested *every feature* every time. And so if you expected to only change feature A and feature D flagged a diff, you'd know there was an issue.

And because adding feature coverage was now as easy as changing or adding a string, adding new features or changing the benchmark stream for a feature (streams got deprecated/outdated constantly, this is live streaming) was trivial.

Once the system was live and integrated into the process, the standard allotment was 2 points (1 engineer day) and anyone on the team could do it.

The last project I worked on is really annoying to explain. 

We had a lot of events from our streams. As in, literal log lines. They could be many things. But we mainly cared about "Stream Down" and "Stream Up". The streams were grouped in groups of 4, or sometimes 2, and there were regions and things that made for additional groupings.

But the main design requirement was that if all 4 origins were down simultaneously, an "outage" began. When the first one came back, it ended. 

The task was to count/track these outages. But I didn't get this project as a greenfield. I inherited it as supposedly fully working. And I just had to change the data source. This was a lie. I ended up having to rebuild the entire thing by the end of it.

But there are 2 things I'm proud of.

First, the script I was given was probably the worst code I have literally ever seen in my life. And it took 4 hours to run because it was basically a nested loop comparing every line to every line.

My algorithm worked by storing "up" and "down" as booleans in a list per stream, so it was a list of 2 or 4 booleans. Then in order to compute "is_in_outage()", we summed the booleans and compared against the number of origins (which we had stored as a known value in a database that was being consumed). If the values matched, no outage, if they didn't, outage. (I don't remember which way the bits went, but it doesn't matter).

This, plus a couple other optimizations allowed me to do it in a single pass. And I could process 4x as much data in just under 10 minutes.

The other thing I did was create an "outage ID" which became the primary key for the database (the original project didn't use a database, it was a fucking disaster). The outage ID was the MD5 hash of the entire outage object (start, end, and some other data) minus the ID itself.

This ensured that the system was idempotent. You could run and upsert as many times as you wanted without duplicating entries. And since there ended up being thousands of outages, many of which were sub-second, those duplicates would quickly poison the data into soup.

One of the main things I'm trying to figure out is how to break the reliance on the LLM to generate every token. That's expensive and horrifically unreliable in the long run. But the issue is that text isn't really a deterministic action space.
